name: Bitmask Dynamic Programming
tagline: Compressing subsets of n <= 20 items into integer bitmasks to turn O(n!) permutations into O(n 2^n) or O(n^2 2^n) DP.
purpose: Build a progressive mental model of bitmask DP—from Held-Karp TSP and canonical assignment to O(3^n) submask iteration and O(n 2^n) SOS DP.

spark.summary: Bitmask DP encodes a subset of n <= 20 elements as an integer 0 .. 2^n - 1, turning exponential factorial permutations (n!) into polynomial-in-subset DP (O(n^2 2^n) or O(n 2^n)).
spark.keyTakeaway: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set (n <= 20) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Held-Karp TSP State Compression (0001 -> 0011 -> 0111 -> 1111) (MASK 0001 -> MASK 0011 -> MASK 1111); Choosing Bitmask DP Pattern by Input Bound n (n <= 20: O(n 2^n) -> n <= 18: O(n^2 2^n) -> n <= 15: O(3^n) -> SOS DP: O(n 2^n)); Selinger Bitmask Join-Order DP (Subsets of Relations) (Join Plan (1111) -> Left Subplan (0011) -> Right Subplan (1100) -> Base Scans).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Scale beyond $n = 20$ by exploiting linearity or splitting the set in half. Relational database query planners (PostgreSQL `geqo_threshold`, DuckDB) use **bitmask DP (Selinger / DPccp)** to pick the optimal join tree across $n$ tables!

**Failure Modes & Application:** Connect bitmask state compression to bitwise tricks, query planners, and graph algorithms.

learningJourney.title: What is Bitmask Dynamic Programming

explanation.foundation: When a problem's optimal substructure depends only on *which* subset $S$ of $n$ items has been used (and optionally the last item), all permutations of $S$ collapse into a single DP state. **Bitmask DP** encodes $S \subseteq \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ as an $n$-bit integer `mask` where bit $i$ is `1` iff item $i \in S$.
explanation.core: Setting one unvisited bit (`mask | (1 << j)`) strictly increases the integer value of `mask`, giving a built-in topological DAG order over `0 .. (1 << n) - 1` and reducing $n!$ permutations to $O(n 2^n)$ or $O(n^2 2^n)$.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Bitmask Compression (and complexity/memory traps)

explanation.foundation: At $n = 18$, $18! \approx 6.4 \times 10^{15}$ is impossible, whereas $18^2 \cdot 2^{18} \approx 8.5 \times 10^7$ runs in under a second.
explanation.core:
Watch three classic pitfalls:
1. **Accidental $O(4^n)$ Submask Loop**: Iterating `0..2^n-1` inside `0..2^n-1` takes $1.07 \times 10^9$ ops at $n=15$, whereas `sub = (sub - 1) & mask` takes $O(3^n) \approx 1.4 \times 10^7$.
2. **Redundant Dimension in Assignment**: When assigning item `i` to worker `k`, you only need `dp[mask]` (not `dp[i][mask]`) because `popcount(mask)` uniquely determines `i`!
3. **OOM on 2D `long` Tables**: `long[1 << 20][20]` uses 160 MB.

decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.

decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

advanced.finalSummary: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set (n <= 20) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
advanced.summary: Bitmask DP encodes a subset of n <= 20 elements as an integer 0 .. 2^n - 1, turning exponential factorial permutations (n!) into polynomial-in-subset DP (O(n^2 2^n) or O(n 2^n)).
advanced.keyTakeaway: Whenever a problem tracks which items from a small set (n <= 20) have been visited or assigned, pack the subset into an integer bitmask and transition by setting one bit at a time.
